name: Ramadan fasting

lead: Ramadan fasting means abstaining from food and drink between dawn and sunset for about 29 or 30 days, with a pre-dawn meal (suhur) and a sunset meal (iftar). For most observers it is a religious practice, but in fitness and looksmaxxing circles it is also discussed as an intermittent-fasting pattern that can change body weight, body composition and hormone rhythms.

Meta-analyses of healthy adults report modest average weight loss and changes in blood lipids, which is why it is discussed for leaning out. Results vary widely with fasting hours, meal size and sleep, and looksmax.org users disagree about whether it helps or harms growth hormone, sleep and physique.

paras: Observers eat before dawn and again after sunset, with fasting lengths of roughly 11 to 16 hours in most places. Many continue lifting or other training during the month, and a randomised trial has compared training before versus after the evening meal. Exemptions exist for travellers, the ill, pregnant or breastfeeding women, the elderly and children.

Studies describe disrupted sleep and circadian patterns, dehydration risk, and elevated risks for people with diabetes, kidney disease or adrenal insufficiency, for whom medical guidance exists. Heavy eating at iftar can offset weight loss, and reported athletic performance drops in some studies. People with medical conditions are advised by clinicians to seek guidance.

angle.text: People who fast for Ramadan often see a modest drop in weight over the month, and some use the period to lean out or reset eating habits. Outcomes depend heavily on what is eaten at suhur and iftar, how well people sleep and whether they keep training.

lead: Ramadan fasting is the practice of abstaining from food, drink and certain behaviours from dawn to sunset throughout Ramadan, the ninth month of the Islamic lunar calendar, which lasts 29 or 30 days. It is one of the five pillars of Islam and is observed by about 1.8 billion Muslims.[1] Most fast for 11 to 16 hours a day, eating suhur before dawn and breaking the fast at iftar.[2]

For people interested in appearance, Ramadan is relevant because the daily eating window resembles time-restricted eating, which can lower body weight and change fat mass. Meta-analyses of healthy adults have examined weight and body composition changes across the month.[3][4] Observers who train often keep lifting through Ramadan, and researchers have studied how the timing of resistance training relative to meals affects strength and muscle size.[5]

Researchers note that findings on health effects are mixed because studies differ in fasting hours, the share of participants who fasted, and what people ate.[6] Looksmax.org users debate whether Ramadan fasting resembles growth-hormone-boosting intermittent fasting, with some saying the night-time eating and disrupted sleep cancel any benefit.[7]

Shifts about 10 to 11 days earlier each solar year

paras: The fast runs from dawn until sunset, with a pre-dawn meal and a sunset meal that traditionally begins with dates. Start dates depend on moon sighting or calculation, so countries can differ by about a day, and because the lunar year is 10 to 11 days shorter than the solar year the month moves through the seasons.[2] In polar regions the fast can exceed 22 hours, and some observers follow the timetable of Mecca or the nearest city with a normal day.[2]

sections.h: Effects on body weight and composition
paras: A meta-analysis of 30 studies of healthy people found changes in blood lipids and body weight after Ramadan.[3] A systematic review of weight and body composition in healthy non-athlete adults examined the same question,[4] and Wikipedia states that weight loss is usually modest and may be regained.[2]

Reviews of fasting physiology describe a shift toward fat as an energy source and the preservation of carbohydrate during fasts, including religious fasts such as Ramadan.[8] Studies of timing show Ramadan alters endocrine and neuroendocrine circadian patterns,[9] and a systematic review of time-restricted eating strategies, including Ramadan, examined effects on cortisol and melatonin.[10]

A randomised controlled trial of 40 men compared the time of day of resistance training during Ramadan intermittent fasting and its effects on strength and muscle growth.[5] Wikipedia reports that a study of Algerian professional footballers found declines in speed, agility and endurance during the month.[2]

Wikipedia notes pregnancy risks and possible kidney injury in people with moderate or severe kidney disease, and some education departments in Berlin and the UK discourage student fasting because of concentration problems.[2] Consensus recommendations exist for managing diabetes during Ramadan.[11][1] Heavy eating at suhur and iftar may reduce any benefit.[2]

On looksmax.org the topic appears mainly through arguments about whether Ramadan fasting provides the same hormonal effects as intermittent fasting; one poster says night-time bingeing, no water and disrupted sleep make it detrimental, while a reply jokes that it carries social benefits with Muslim women.[7]

Many studies exist. A meta-analysis of healthy people reports changes in LDL cholesterol and body weight,[3] a cross-sectional study of 50 healthy subjects reports lower proinflammatory cytokines during Ramadan intermittent fasting,[12] and a review of religious fasting concludes findings are mixed because of differences in fasting hours and diet.[6] A randomised trial examined training timing and muscle outcomes.[5]

lore.intro: In looksmaxxing forums, Ramadan appears as a comparison point for intermittent fasting and growth hormone.[7]
